To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have discovered a novel OFD1 mutation in the exons 20/21 region of the gene that causes primary ciliary dyskenesia without other syndromic symptoms, and we have found that this mutation causes a defect in the respiratory epithelial cilia but not the brain primary cilia.
(i) mutations in exons of the OFD gene can cause PCD, (ii) these patients do not have the symptoms characteristic for syndromes caused by other OFD1 mutations

we found novel OFD1 mutations in exons20 and 21 in PCD patients, that the C-terminus of OFD1 is important for ciliary function, that the OFD1 gene should be included in PCD screening, and that OFD1 mutations cause PCD without severe syndromic symptoms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel form of syndromic PDC, in which the typical symptoms of OFD1-related disorders are missing.
the role of motility of the cilia in the development of the PCD respiratory phenotype and with the role of the OFD protein in the development and function of cilia.
the role of the motile cilia in the pathomechanism of PCD, and it also contributes to the understanding of the molecular pathogenesis of the OFD family of syndromes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
OFD1 is a gene for syndromic PBD, but that the phenotype is highly variable and that the respiratory phenotype is dominant.
mutations in OFD1 cause syndromic PDC, but that the syndromic symptoms are not obligatory.
OFD1 is a ciliopathy gene, but it should not be considered a PCD gene, as the majority of mutations in OFD1 cause syndromic ciliary disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
OFD1 mutations in exons encoding for the C-terminal part (exons 20-22) of the protein lead to PCD without the presence of other syndromic symptoms.
the OFD1 gene should be included in a panel for mutation screening in patients with PCD and in the workup of patients with a typical PFD phenotype and a negative result of the PCD panel.
mutations of the C-terminal region of OFD1 cause PCD with or without syndromic symptoms and that the severity of the phenotype is determined by the specific location of the mutation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
OFD1 is a ciliary gene, and its mutations may lead to PCD, even in the absence of other symptoms.
OFD1 mutations can cause PCD with a variable degree of associated syndromic features.
the C-terminus of OFD1 is crucial for the function of motile ciliaries.
